title: Makli: the city of the dead in Sindh
lines: On a low hill near Thatta, in Sindh, lies one of the largest cemeteries in the world. This is Makli.
The necropolis stretches along a plateau about six and a half kilometres long.
Estimates of its graves range from about one hundred and twenty-five thousand to half a million.
Burials here began in the fourteenth century, and continued for around four hundred years.
Thatta was then the capital of Sindh, ruled in turn by the Samma, Arghun and Tarkhan dynasties, and later by the Mughals.
Kings, queens, saints, scholars and poets were buried here.
One of the finest tombs belongs to Jam Nizamuddin the Second, who ruled Sindh from fourteen sixty-one to fifteen-oh-nine. Its stone carvings blend Hindu and Islamic designs.
Later tombs, like those of Isa Khan Tarkhan and Diwan Shurfa Khan, are decorated with glazed tiles and fine brickwork.
In nineteen eighty-one, UNESCO listed the Historical Monuments at Makli as a World Heritage Site.
But the site is under threat from salty winds, heavy rain, encroachment and neglect, and UNESCO says funding for its care is inadequate.
It remains a remarkable record of Sindh's history, written in stone.
